Proper & Improper Fractions.answer: (3×4)+1=13, so 3 1/4 = 13/4 — confirming the two fractions are indeed equal.

Proper & Improper Fractions.q: A scientist records a measurement as 58/9 units. Without fully converting, explain how you can quickly estimate the whole number part of the equivalent mixed fraction.
Proper & Improper Fractions.answer: You can estimate by finding the largest multiple of 9 that is less than or equal to 58 (which is 54=9×6), telling you the whole number part is at least 6 before doing the exact division to confirm.

Proper & Improper Fractions.q: A fabric roll is labelled with length 8 3/10 metres for a tailoring order. Convert this into an improper fraction to use in a cutting calculation.
Why might converting BOTH fractions in a comparison (e.g., comparing 3 1/2 and 17/5) to the SAME form (either both mixed or both improper) make the comparison easier?
Proper & Improper Fractions.answer: Having both fractions in the same form allows for a direct, fair comparison method (like comparing improper fraction numerators with the same denominator, or comparing whole number parts first in mixed form) rather than trying to mentally juggle two different representations at once.

Proper & Improper Fractions.q: A 7 2/3 hour work shift needs to be expressed as an improper fraction for payroll calculation software. Convert it.
A water reservoir’s capacity is described as 91/12 million litres. Convert this to a mixed fraction, and explain what the fractional part (in twelfths) might represent practically.
Proper & Improper Fractions.answer: 91÷12=7 remainder 7, so 91/12=7 7/12 million litres — the fractional part 7/12 represents a partial amount beyond the 7 full million-litre units, useful for precise capacity tracking.

Proper & Improper Fractions.q: A printing press uses 5 7/8 reams of paper for one project and 3 3/8 reams for another. Convert BOTH mixed fractions into improper fractions.
Why might it be useful, in the previous paper-usage scenario, to convert both quantities to improper fractions with the SAME denominator before any further calculation (like finding the total used)?
Proper & Improper Fractions.answer: Having the same denominator allows you to simply add the numerators directly to find a combined total (47/8 + 27/8 = 74/8), rather than needing to separately manage whole numbers and fraction parts during the calculation.

Proper & Improper Fractions.q: A 105/13 metre rope needs to be cut for a project. Convert this improper fraction into a mixed fraction, explaining each step.
A chemistry experiment requires 9 4/5 ml of a solution, but the digital measuring tool only accepts improper fraction input. Convert 9 4/5 accordingly.
Why would a digital tool or computer program often prefer working with improper fractions internally, even if it DISPLAYS results to users as mixed fractions?
Proper & Improper Fractions.answer: Improper fractions are mathematically simpler and more consistent for a program to perform calculations (addition, multiplication, etc.) with a single numerator and denominator, while converting to mixed fraction format only at the final display stage makes results more human-readable.

Proper & Improper Fractions.q: A 121/15 cm length needs measuring on a ruler marked only in whole centimetres and fractions. Convert this improper fraction to a mixed fraction.
A trader claims a sack weighs "6 and a bit" kilograms, more precisely written as 6 5/7 kg. Convert this claim into an improper fraction for record-keeping.

Fractions on Number Line.q: To mark 3/7 on a number line, into how many equal parts should the segment from 0 to 1 be divided?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: 7 equal parts, matching the denominator.

Fractions on Number Line.q: After dividing 0 to 1 into 7 equal parts, which mark represents 3/7?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: The 3rd mark counting from 0, matching the numerator.

Fractions on Number Line.q: Where does the fraction 1/2 lie on a number line from 0 to 1?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: Exactly halfway between 0 and 1.

Fractions on Number Line.q: Explain step by step how to mark the fraction 2/5 on a number line.
steps: Draw a line segment from 0 to 1.
Divide the segment into 5 equal parts (denominator).
Mark the 2nd point from 0 (numerator) — this is 2/5.
Fractions on Number Line.answer: 2/5 is marked at the 2nd point when the segment from 0 to 1 is divided into 5 equal parts.

Fractions on Number Line.q: Between which two whole numbers does the improper fraction 7/2 lie?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: 7÷2=3 remainder 1, so 7/2=3 1/2, lying between the whole numbers 3 and 4.

Fractions on Number Line.q: Between which two whole numbers does the improper fraction 10/3 lie?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: 10÷3=3 remainder 1, so 10/3=3 1/3, lying between the whole numbers 3 and 4.

Fractions on Number Line.q: On a number line, fraction X is at 3/8 and fraction Y is at 6/8. Which fraction is positioned further to the right?
Why does a fraction further to the right on a number line always represent a larger value?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: A number line is ordered from smaller values (left) to larger values (right) — so any point further right always represents a bigger number, fractions included.

Fractions on Number Line.q: If two different fractions are marked at the EXACT same point on a number line, what must be true about them?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: They must be equivalent fractions, since they represent the same value despite possibly looking different.

Fractions on Number Line.q: Mark 5/6 on a number line by describing the process step by step.
steps: Count 5 parts from 0 and mark that point — this is 5/6.
Fractions on Number Line.answer: 5/6 is found by dividing 0-to-1 into 6 equal parts and marking the 5th point from 0.

Fractions on Number Line.q: Why is it important that ALL the parts between 0 and 1 are EQUAL when marking a fraction on a number line?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: If the parts were unequal, the marks would not correctly represent the fraction’s true value — fractions assume equal-sized divisions of the whole.

Fractions on Number Line.q: A number line has whole numbers 0, 1, and 2 marked. Where would 5/4 be located?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: 5/4=1 1/4, so it would be located between 1 and 2, a quarter of the way past 1.

Fractions on Number Line.q: Why does the number line continue past 1 to represent improper fractions like 5/4 or 7/3?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: Improper fractions represent values of 1 or more, so the number line needs to extend beyond 1 (into 2, 3, etc.) to show their exact position.

Fractions on Number Line.q: Two points on a number line represent 3/10 and 7/10. Which point is closer to 1?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: 7/10 is closer to 1, since it is a larger fraction (closer to the value 1) than 3/10.

Fractions on Number Line.q: Why might placing fractions on a number line help students UNDERSTAND fraction comparisons better than just looking at the numbers alone?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: A number line gives a visual, spatial representation of fraction size, making it intuitively clear which fraction is bigger by simply seeing which one is positioned further to the right.

Fractions on Number Line.q: To mark 4/9 on a number line, how many equal parts should the segment from 0 to 1 be divided into, and which mark represents 4/9?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: Divide into 9 equal parts; the 4th mark from 0 represents 4/9.

Fractions on Number Line.q: Between which two whole numbers does 17/5 lie on a number line?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: 17÷5=3 remainder 2, so 17/5=3 2/5, lying between the whole numbers 3 and 4.

Fractions on Number Line.q: A number line position is marked exactly at the tick for 2. What fraction (with denominator 3) would represent this same position?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: 6/3, since 6÷3=2 exactly — this fraction equals exactly 2 whole units.

Fractions on Number Line.q: On a number line, 1/6 is marked closer to 0, and 5/6 is marked closer to 1. What does this tell you about comparing 1/6 and 5/6?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: It confirms that 1/6 < 5/6, since the fraction closer to 0 is the smaller value.

Fractions on Number Line.q: Explain step by step how to determine the number-line position of the improper fraction 11/4.
steps: Convert to a mixed fraction: 11÷4=2 remainder 3, so 11/4=2 3/4.
Identify the whole number part: 2, meaning the position is between 2 and 3.
Identify the fraction part: 3/4, meaning the position is three-quarters of the way from 2 to 3.
Fractions on Number Line.answer: 11/4 is located three-quarters of the way between the whole numbers 2 and 3 on the number line.

Fractions on Number Line.q: Why is converting an improper fraction to a MIXED fraction a helpful first step before placing it on a number line?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: The whole number part of the mixed fraction immediately tells you WHICH segment (e.g., between 2 and 3) to look in, making the placement process much simpler.

Fractions on Number Line.q: A number line shows points for 2/7 and 2/5. Without finding a common denominator, can you guess which might be larger, and why might this be tricky?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: It can be tricky to guess directly since the numerators are the same (2) but the denominators differ — generally, with the same numerator, the fraction with the SMALLER denominator (2/5) is larger, since the whole is divided into fewer, larger parts.

Fractions on Number Line.q: Why does this chapter’s number-line method work the same way regardless of whether the denominator is small (like 2) or large (like 12)?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: The method — dividing the 0-to-1 segment into equal parts matching the denominator, then counting parts matching the numerator — is a universal process that works consistently no matter how large or small the denominator is.

Fractions on Number Line.q: A point on a number line is exactly midway between the marks for 1/4 and 3/4. What fraction would this point likely represent?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: It would represent 1/2 (2/4), since 1/2 lies exactly midway between 1/4 and 3/4.

Fractions on Number Line.q: Mark the improper fraction 13/6 on a number line, explaining your steps.
steps: Convert to a mixed fraction: 13÷6=2 remainder 1, so 13/6=2 1/6.
This means the position lies between the whole numbers 2 and 3.
Specifically, it is one-sixth of the way from 2 to 3.
Fractions on Number Line.answer: 13/6 is located one-sixth of the way between the whole numbers 2 and 3.

Fractions on Number Line.q: Why might a teacher use a number line to teach BOTH proper and improper fractions together?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: A number line shows that proper and improper fractions are simply different positions along the SAME continuous line, helping students see they are part of one connected number system rather than two separate, unrelated ideas.

Fractions on Number Line.q: A number line position is marked at the same point as both 3/4 and 6/8. What does this confirm about these two fractions?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: It confirms that 3/4 and 6/8 are equivalent fractions, since they occupy the exact same position (representing the same value).

Fractions on Number Line.q: Why can a number line have INFINITELY many fraction points between any two whole numbers, like 0 and 1?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: Because fractions can have any whole number as a denominator, and for each denominator there are multiple possible numerators, creating endless possible positions between any two points on the line.

Fractions on Number Line.q: A point on the number line is positioned just slightly to the left of the mark for 1. What might this suggest about the fraction at that point?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: It suggests the fraction is a proper fraction very close to 1 in value, such as 9/10 or 11/12 — close to but still less than a whole.

Fractions on Number Line.q: A number line marked from 0 to 3 needs the fraction 8/3 placed on it. Explain step by step how to find its position.
steps: Convert to a mixed fraction: 8÷3=2 remainder 2, so 8/3=2 2/3.
This tells us the position lies between the whole numbers 2 and 3.
Specifically, it is two-thirds of the way from 2 to 3.
Fractions on Number Line.answer: 8/3 is located two-thirds of the way between the whole numbers 2 and 3 on the number line.

Fractions on Number Line.q: Why might engineers or designers use number-line-style scales (like rulers marked in fractions of an inch) in real-world tools?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: A number-line-style scale allows for precise, visual measurement of fractional quantities, making it easy to read off exact fractional positions (like 3/8 inch) directly from a physical tool.

Fractions on Number Line.q: Two ships are tracked on a 0-to-1 journey-progress number line: Ship A at 5/9 and Ship B at 7/9. A third ship, Ship C, is reported to be exactly between them. What fraction (with denominator 9) would represent Ship C’s position?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: Exactly between 5/9 and 7/9 (using a common denominator of 9) would be 6/9, the midpoint.

Fractions on Number Line.q: Why is it mathematically true that the midpoint between two LIKE fractions (like 5/9 and 7/9) is simply the AVERAGE of their numerators, over the same denominator?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: Since both fractions share the same denominator, finding the middle position is the same as finding the middle of their numerators (5 and 7, averaging to 6) while keeping the denominator unchanged — giving 6/9.

Fractions on Number Line.q: A number line from 0 to 5 needs several improper fractions placed on it: 7/2, 13/4, and 22/5. Convert ALL THREE to mixed fractions to determine which whole-number segment each belongs in.
Fractions on Number Line.answer: 7/2 and 13/4 both lie between 3 and 4, while 22/5 lies between 4 and 5.

Fractions on Number Line.q: Of the three fractions in the previous question (7/2=3 1/2, 13/4=3 1/4, 22/5=4 2/5), which is the SMALLEST?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: 13/4 (3 1/4) is the smallest, since 3 1/4 < 3 1/2 < 4 2/5.

Fractions on Number Line.q: Why might placing MULTIPLE improper fractions on the SAME number line (as in the previous questions) be a particularly powerful way to compare them all at once?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: A shared number line visually shows the relative order and spacing of ALL the fractions simultaneously, making it easy to compare any pair (or all of them together) without needing separate calculations for every possible pair.

Fractions on Number Line.q: A number line application tracks rainfall as a fraction of a fixed daily maximum. If today’s rainfall is marked at 11/8 of the usual daily average, what does a position PAST the “1” mark tell us?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: A position past the “1” mark (since 11/8 is an improper fraction, greater than 1) tells us that today’s rainfall EXCEEDED the usual daily average.

Fractions on Number Line.q: Why might real-world data (like rainfall, stock prices relative to a baseline, or exam scores relative to a pass mark) sometimes be naturally represented using fractions or ratios GREATER than 1 on a number-line-style scale?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: When a real-world quantity EXCEEDS a reference point or baseline (like average rainfall or a pass mark), expressing it as an improper fraction (greater than 1) naturally and accurately shows that it has surpassed that baseline value.

Fractions on Number Line.q: A number line from 0 to 2 has a point marked at exactly 1.5 units, found to correspond to an unknown fraction with denominator 4. What is this fraction?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: 1.5 = 3/2, and converting to fourths: 3/2 = 6/4. So the fraction (with denominator 4) is 6/4.

Fractions on Number Line.q: Why does the SAME position on a number line often have MULTIPLE valid fraction representations, as seen in the previous question (3/2 = 6/4)?
Fractions on Number Line.answer: Since equivalent fractions all represent the same value, any single position on a number line can correctly be labeled with infinitely many different (but equivalent) fractions, depending on which denominator is chosen.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: What are equivalent fractions?
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: Equivalent fractions are different fractions that represent the same value or the same part of a whole.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: How do you find an equivalent fraction of a given fraction?
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: Multiply (or divide) both the numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Find an equivalent fraction of 1/3 by multiplying numerator and denominator by 3.
Find an equivalent fraction of 2/5 by multiplying numerator and denominator by 4.
What is the simplest form of a fraction?
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: The form where the numerator and denominator have no common factor other than 1.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Simplify 6/8 to its lowest form.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: HCF of 6 and 8 is 2. Dividing both by 2: 6/8 = 3/4.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Simplify 9/12 to its lowest form.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: HCF of 9 and 12 is 3. Dividing both by 3: 9/12 = 3/4.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Are 2/6 and 1/3 equivalent fractions? Explain.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: Yes, because dividing both numerator and denominator of 2/6 by 2 (their HCF) gives 1/3, the simplest form.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Explain step by step how to find an equivalent fraction of 4/7 by multiplying by 5.
Explain step by step how to simplify the fraction 15/20 to its lowest form.
steps: Find the HCF of 15 and 20: HCF=5.
Divide the numerator by the HCF: 15÷5=3.
Divide the denominator by the HCF: 20÷5=4, giving the simplified fraction 3/4.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: 15/20 simplifies to 3/4.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Why does multiplying both numerator and denominator by the same number NOT change the value of the fraction?
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: Because this is the same as multiplying the fraction by a fraction equal to 1 (like 5/5 or 3/3) — and multiplying any number by 1 does not change its value.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Is the fraction 5/9 in its simplest form? Explain why or why not.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: Yes, 5/9 is in simplest form because 5 and 9 share no common factor other than 1 (5 is prime and does not divide 9).

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Find two different equivalent fractions of 3/4 by multiplying by 2 and by 5 separately.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: Multiplying by 2: 3/4 = 6/8. Multiplying by 5: 3/4 = 15/20.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Simplify the fraction 24/36 to its lowest form.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: HCF of 24 and 36 is 12. Dividing both by 12: 24/36 = 2/3.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: A recipe originally needing 2/3 cup of milk is doubled. Express the doubled amount as an equivalent fraction with denominator 6.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: Multiplying 2/3 by 2/2 gives 4/6 — but since the recipe is doubled, the actual amount needed is 4/3 cups (a separate calculation), while 4/6 remains just an equivalent of the original 2/3.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Why might a baker want to convert a fraction like 3/4 cup into an equivalent fraction with a larger denominator, such as 12, when using a measuring cup marked in twelfths?
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: Converting to twelfths (9/12) allows the baker to measure precisely using the markings available on that particular measuring cup, since the original quarter markings might not be present.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Simplify 30/45 to its lowest form.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: HCF of 30 and 45 is 15. Dividing both by 15: 30/45 = 2/3.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Find an equivalent fraction of 5/6 by multiplying numerator and denominator by 3.
Simplify 16/24 to its lowest form.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: HCF of 16 and 24 is 8. Dividing both by 8: 16/24 = 2/3.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Two students simplify 12/18 differently: one divides by 2 first to get 6/9, then by 3 to get 2/3. The other divides directly by 6 to get 2/3. Are both methods valid?
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: Yes, both methods are valid. Dividing step by step by smaller common factors (2, then 3) eventually reaches the same simplest form as dividing directly by the HCF (6).

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Why is dividing directly by the HCF generally faster than simplifying in multiple smaller steps?
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: Dividing by the HCF reduces the fraction to its simplest form in just ONE step, while dividing by smaller common factors may require MULTIPLE steps to reach the same final simplified result.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Find the HCF of 21 and 28, and use it to simplify 21/28.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: HCF of 21 and 28 is 7. Dividing both by 7: 21/28 = 3/4.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: A fraction 7/7 represents what value, and is it considered to be in simplest form?
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: 7/7 equals exactly 1 whole. It IS in simplest form, since the HCF of 7 and 7 is 7 itself, and dividing both by 7 gives 1/1, which still represents the value 1.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Simplify 40/50 to its lowest form.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: HCF of 40 and 50 is 10. Dividing both by 10: 40/50 = 4/5.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: A survey shows 36/48 of respondents prefer one brand. Simplify this fraction.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: HCF of 36 and 48 is 12. Dividing both by 12: 36/48 = 3/4.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Explain step by step how to check whether 14/21 and 2/3 are equivalent fractions.
steps: Simplify 14/21 by finding its HCF: HCF of 14 and 21 is 7.
Divide both numerator and denominator by 7: 14÷7=2, 21÷7=3.
Compare the result (2/3) to the given fraction (2/3) — they match, confirming equivalence.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: Yes, 14/21 and 2/3 are equivalent, since 14/21 simplifies exactly to 2/3.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Why might TWO completely different-looking fractions, like 5/15 and 8/24, actually be equivalent? Verify using simplification.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: 5/15 simplifies (divide by 5) to 1/3, and 8/24 simplifies (divide by 8) to 1/3 as well — since both reduce to the same simplest form, they are indeed equivalent.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: A ribbon company sells ribbon in lengths described as 9/12 metre or 3/4 metre. Are these the same length? Verify.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: Yes — simplifying 9/12 (divide by 3, their HCF) gives 3/4, confirming both descriptions refer to the same length.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Simplify 28/35 to its lowest form.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: HCF of 28 and 35 is 7. Dividing both by 7: 28/35 = 4/5.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Why would simplifying fractions before comparing or adding them often make calculations easier?
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: Smaller numbers (after simplification) are easier to work with mentally and reduce the chance of calculation errors, especially when finding common denominators or comparing multiple fractions.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: A juice mix uses 18/24 part juice concentrate. Simplify this ratio-like fraction.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: HCF of 18 and 24 is 6. Dividing both by 6: 18/24 = 3/4.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Find an equivalent fraction of 7/8 with a denominator of 32.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: 32÷8=4, so multiply numerator and denominator by 4: 7×4=28, giving 28/32.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: A test score is reported as 17/25 in one class and an equivalent score is needed out of 100 for a school-wide report. Find the equivalent fraction with denominator 100.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: 100÷25=4, so multiply numerator and denominator by 4: 17×4=68, giving 68/100.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: A trader has two coils of wire, one measuring 25/40 metre, and wants the simplest form for a price list. Simplify 25/40.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: HCF of 25 and 40 is 5. Dividing both by 5: 25/40 = 5/8.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Why might a company prefer displaying measurements in their SIMPLEST fraction form on a price list, rather than a more complicated equivalent fraction?
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: Simplest form fractions are easier for customers to read, understand, and compare at a glance, reducing confusion compared to seeing unnecessarily large numerators and denominators.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: A survey of 84 people found 63 prefer outdoor activities. Express this as a fraction and simplify it to its lowest form.
steps: Find the HCF of 63 and 84: HCF=21.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: 63/84 simplifies to 3/4.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Two test results, 45/60 and 27/36, are claimed to represent the same score percentage. Verify by simplifying both.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: 45/60 simplifies (HCF=15) to 3/4. 27/36 simplifies (HCF=9) to 3/4. Both simplify to the same value, confirming the claim.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Why is it mathematically guaranteed that any fraction has INFINITELY many equivalent fractions?
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: Since you can multiply the numerator and denominator by ANY non-zero whole number (1, 2, 3, 4, and so on, without limit), there is no end to how many equivalent versions of a fraction can be created.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: A factory produces parts where 72/96 pass quality control. Simplify this pass-rate fraction to its lowest form.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: HCF of 72 and 96 is 24. Dividing both by 24: 72/96 = 3/4.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: A map scale uses the fraction 1/50000 to represent distances. Why would simplifying or changing this fraction’s form (like to 2/100000) NOT be useful in this context, even though it is mathematically equivalent?
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: While mathematically equivalent, 2/100000 is not in simplest form and uses unnecessarily larger numbers — the original 1/50000 is already simplest and more practical for quick reading and calculation by map users.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: A school reports that 56/70 of students passed an exam. Simplify this fraction, showing your steps.
steps: Find the HCF of 56 and 70: HCF=14.
Divide the numerator by the HCF: 56÷14=4.
Divide the denominator by the HCF: 70÷14=5, giving 4/5.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: 56/70 simplifies to 4/5.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Why might two fractions that look very different at first, like 11/121, actually simplify to a much simpler fraction? Check by simplifying 11/121.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: HCF of 11 and 121 is 11 (since 121=11×11). Dividing both by 11 gives 1/11 — showing that large-looking fractions can sometimes hide a much simpler underlying value.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: A study finds 95/100 of equivalent fraction practice problems can be solved using the HCF method. Simplify 95/100.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: HCF of 95 and 100 is 5. Dividing both by 5: 95/100 = 19/20.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: A 144/180 scale model ratio needs simplifying for an engineering report. Find the simplest form, showing your steps.
steps: Find the HCF of 144 and 180: HCF=36.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: 144/180 simplifies to 4/5.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Why might engineers specifically need the SIMPLEST form of a ratio/fraction (like 4/5 instead of 144/180) when communicating scale models to colleagues?
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: Simplest form numbers are far easier to mentally process, communicate verbally, and use in further quick calculations, reducing the chance of miscommunication or calculation errors compared to large unsimplified numbers.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: A 51/68 fraction needs simplifying for a textbook example. Find its simplest form.
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: HCF of 51 and 68 is 17. Dividing both by 17: 51/68 = 3/4.

Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.q: Why does the METHOD for finding equivalent fractions (multiply/divide both parts equally) work the same way regardless of how large or small the original fraction’s numbers are?
Equivalent Fractions & Simplest Form.answer: The underlying mathematical principle — that multiplying or dividing both numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number preserves the fraction’s VALUE — is a universal rule that applies consistently to any fraction, no matter its size.

Comparing Fractions.q: What are like fractions?
Comparing Fractions.answer: Fractions that have the same denominator.

Comparing Fractions.q: What are unlike fractions?
Comparing Fractions.answer: Fractions that have different denominators.

Comparing Fractions.q: How do you compare two like fractions?
Comparing Fractions.answer: Simply compare their numerators — the larger numerator means the larger fraction.

Comparing Fractions.q: Compare 4/9 and 7/9. Which is larger?
Comparing Fractions.answer: 7/9 is larger, since both have denominator 9, and 7 > 4.

Comparing Fractions.q: Compare 2/11 and 5/11. Which is smaller?
Comparing Fractions.answer: 2/11 is smaller, since both have denominator 11, and 2 < 5.

Comparing Fractions.q: What is the first step when comparing two unlike fractions?
Comparing Fractions.answer: Find the LCM of their denominators and convert both fractions to like fractions using that LCM.

Comparing Fractions.q: Find the LCM of 3 and 5, needed to compare fractions with these denominators.
Comparing Fractions.answer: The LCM of 3 and 5 is 15.

Comparing Fractions.q: Compare 1/3 and 2/5 using LCM 15 (1/3=5/15, 2/5=6/15). Which is larger?
Comparing Fractions.answer: 2/5 (6/15) is larger than 1/3 (5/15), since 6 > 5.

Comparing Fractions.q: Compare 3/4 and 5/8 using a common denominator of 8 (3/4=6/8). Which is larger?
Comparing Fractions.answer: 3/4 (6/8) is larger than 5/8, since 6 > 5.

Comparing Fractions.q: Explain step by step how to compare 5/6 and 7/9.
steps: Find the LCM of 6 and 9: LCM=18.
Comparing Fractions.answer: 5/6 is larger than 7/9.

Comparing Fractions.q: Explain step by step how to arrange 1/4, 3/8, and 1/2 from smallest to largest.
steps: Find the LCM of 4, 8, and 2: LCM=8.
Comparing Fractions.answer: The order from smallest to largest is 1/4, 3/8, 1/2.

Comparing Fractions.q: Why does comparing numerators directly ONLY work correctly when the fractions already have the same denominator?
Comparing Fractions.answer: The denominator tells us the SIZE of each equal part — if denominators differ, the "parts" being counted by the numerators are different sizes, so comparing numerators alone would be misleading without first making the denominators the same.

Comparing Fractions.q: Arrange 5/12, 1/12, and 8/12 from largest to smallest.
Comparing Fractions.answer: Since all have denominator 12, compare numerators: 8/12 > 5/12 > 1/12.

Comparing Fractions.q: A glass is 5/8 full, another is 3/8 full. Which glass has less water?
Comparing Fractions.answer: The glass with 3/8 has less water, since 3 < 5 (same denominator 8).

Comparing Fractions.q: Compare 2/3 and 3/5 using LCM 15 (2/3=10/15, 3/5=9/15). Which is larger?
Comparing Fractions.answer: 2/3 (10/15) is larger than 3/5 (9/15), since 10 > 9.

Comparing Fractions.q: Why is using the LCM (rather than just any common multiple) generally the most EFFICIENT choice for comparing unlike fractions?
Comparing Fractions.answer: The LCM is the SMALLEST common denominator possible, which keeps the resulting numerators and denominators as small as possible, making the comparison calculation simpler and less error-prone compared to using a larger common multiple.

Comparing Fractions.q: Compare 4/7 and 5/7. State which symbol (<, >, or =) correctly compares them.
Comparing Fractions.answer: 4/7 < 5/7, since both share denominator 7, and 4 < 5.

Comparing Fractions.q: Compare 5/9 and 5/6 using LCM 18 (5/9=10/18, 5/6=15/18). Which is larger?
Comparing Fractions.answer: 5/6 (15/18) is larger than 5/9 (10/18), since 15 > 10.

Comparing Fractions.q: A cross-multiplication check compares a/b and c/d using a×d versus b×c. Apply this to compare 3/4 and 5/7.
Use cross-multiplication to compare 2/9 and 1/5.
Why does cross-multiplication give the SAME result as converting to a common denominator and comparing numerators?
Comparing Fractions.answer: Cross-multiplication is essentially a shortcut: multiplying a×d and b×c produces numbers proportional to what the numerators WOULD be if both fractions were converted to the common denominator of b×d, so the comparison outcome is mathematically identical.

Comparing Fractions.q: Arrange 7/10, 3/10, and 9/10 from smallest to largest.
Comparing Fractions.answer: Since denominators are the same (10), compare numerators: 3/10 < 7/10 < 9/10.

Comparing Fractions.q: Two friends ran different distances: 3/5 km and 7/10 km. Using LCM 10 (3/5=6/10), who ran further?
Comparing Fractions.answer: The friend who ran 7/10 km ran further, since 7/10 > 6/10 (which is 3/5).

Comparing Fractions.q: A baker uses 2/3 cup of sugar in one recipe and 5/8 cup in another. Using LCM 24 (2/3=16/24, 5/8=15/24), which recipe uses more sugar?
Comparing Fractions.answer: The first recipe (2/3 cup = 16/24) uses more sugar than the second (5/8 cup = 15/24), since 16 > 15.

Comparing Fractions.q: Explain step by step how to arrange 5/6, 2/3, and 3/4 from largest to smallest.
steps: Find the LCM of 6, 3, and 4: LCM=12.
Compare numerators (10, 9, 8) to order from largest to smallest: 5/6 > 3/4 > 2/3.
Comparing Fractions.answer: The order from largest to smallest is 5/6, 3/4, 2/3.

Comparing Fractions.q: Why might simply "eyeballing" or guessing which unlike fraction is larger (without converting to a common denominator) often lead to mistakes?
Comparing Fractions.answer: Without a common denominator, the size of each "part" represented by the numerators differs between fractions, making intuitive numerator comparisons unreliable — for example, 3/4 looks like it has a "smaller" numerator than 5/8, but 3/4 is actually the larger fraction.

Comparing Fractions.q: A 3/5 litre bottle and a 7/15 litre bottle are compared using LCM 15 (3/5=9/15). Which bottle holds more?
Comparing Fractions.answer: The 3/5 litre bottle (9/15) holds more than the 7/15 litre bottle, since 9 > 7.

Comparing Fractions.q: Two students score 11/15 and 13/20 in a test (as fractions of total marks). Using LCM 60 (11/15=44/60, 13/20=39/60), who scored higher proportionally?
Comparing Fractions.answer: The student who scored 11/15 (44/60) scored higher proportionally than 13/20 (39/60), since 44 > 39.

Comparing Fractions.q: Why can converting fractions to PERCENTAGES (a later topic) be seen as just another way of comparing fractions using a common "denominator" of 100?
Comparing Fractions.answer: Percentages express every fraction as "out of 100," which is essentially converting all fractions to a common denominator of 100, allowing for the same kind of easy numerator-based comparison used with like fractions.

Comparing Fractions.q: Order 4/9, 1/3, and 5/9 from smallest to largest, using a common denominator of 9 (1/3=3/9).
Comparing Fractions.answer: Comparing numerators 3, 4, 5: 1/3 (3/9) < 4/9 < 5/9.

Comparing Fractions.q: A runner covers 5/8 of a track on day one and 11/16 on day two. Using LCM 16 (5/8=10/16), on which day did the runner cover more distance?
Comparing Fractions.answer: Day two, since 11/16 > 10/16 (which is 5/8).

Comparing Fractions.q: Why is finding a common denominator considered "fair" when comparing fractions, in terms of what it does to each fraction’s parts?
Comparing Fractions.answer: Converting to a common denominator resizes the "parts" of both fractions to be the SAME size, so that comparing the COUNT of parts (numerators) becomes a fair, apples-to-apples comparison.

Comparing Fractions.q: Four containers hold 5/6, 2/3, 7/12, and 3/4 litres. Find a common denominator and arrange from smallest to largest.
steps: Find the LCM of 6, 3, 12, and 4: LCM=12.
Comparing Fractions.answer: The order from smallest to largest is 7/12, 2/3, 3/4, 5/6.

Comparing Fractions.q: Why might comparing FOUR or more unlike fractions at once (as in the previous question) still use the exact same method as comparing just two unlike fractions?
Comparing Fractions.answer: The method — finding a common denominator (LCM of ALL denominators involved) and comparing numerators — scales naturally to any number of fractions, since it converts every fraction into the same "unit size" regardless of how many fractions are being compared.

Comparing Fractions.q: A nutrition label shows two snacks contain 3/8 and 2/5 of the daily recommended sugar. Using LCM 40 (3/8=15/40, 2/5=16/40), which snack has MORE sugar relative to the daily recommendation?
Comparing Fractions.answer: The snack with 2/5 (16/40) has slightly more relative sugar than the one with 3/8 (15/40).

Comparing Fractions.q: Why might nutrition or health-related comparisons (like in the previous question) require especially careful and ACCURATE fraction comparison methods, rather than rough estimates?
Comparing Fractions.answer: Small differences in fractions (like 15/40 versus 16/40) could represent meaningful real-world differences in health impact, so accurate methods (common denominators, not guesswork) help ensure people make informed dietary decisions based on correct comparisons.

Comparing Fractions.q: A 17/24 fraction and an 11/16 fraction are being compared using cross-multiplication. Calculate both cross-products.
A class is divided so that 13/20 are in one activity and 7/10 are in another (likely overlapping group counts in this scenario). Using LCM 20 (7/10=14/20), which group fraction is larger?
Comparing Fractions.answer: 7/10 (14/20) is larger than 13/20, since 14 > 13.

Comparing Fractions.q: Why does cross-multiplication become LESS practical (compared to using LCM and common denominators) when comparing THREE OR MORE fractions at once?
Comparing Fractions.answer: Cross-multiplication is designed for comparing just TWO fractions at a time — comparing three or more fractions would require multiple repeated pairwise cross-multiplications, which becomes more complex and error-prone than simply converting all fractions to one common denominator at once.

Comparing Fractions.q: A 19/30 and 23/36 fraction are compared using LCM 180 (19/30=114/180, 23/36=115/180). Which is larger, and by how much (in 180ths)?
Comparing Fractions.answer: 23/36 (115/180) is larger than 19/30 (114/180), larger by exactly 1/180.

Comparing Fractions.q: Why might VERY CLOSE fraction comparisons, like the previous question (114/180 vs 115/180), be especially important to calculate carefully rather than estimate?
Comparing Fractions.answer: When fractions are very close in value, rough estimation could easily lead to an INCORRECT conclusion about which is larger — precise calculation using a common denominator is necessary to confidently and correctly determine the true comparison.

Comparing Fractions.q: A 5/7 and 8/11 fraction are compared using cross-multiplication. Show the calculation and conclusion.
Comparing Fractions.answer: 5×11=55 and 7×8=56. Since 56 > 55, 8/11 > 5/7 (just barely).

Comparing Fractions.q: Explain step by step how to arrange 7/8, 5/6, 11/12, and 3/4 from LARGEST to smallest.
steps: Find the LCM of 8, 6, 12, and 4: LCM=24.
Order numerators from largest to smallest (22, 21, 20, 18): 11/12 > 7/8 > 5/6 > 3/4.
Comparing Fractions.answer: The order from largest to smallest is 11/12, 7/8, 5/6, 3/4.

Comparing Fractions.q: Why is it useful, when ordering several fractions like in the previous question, to first write out ALL the converted "like fraction" forms together before trying to compare them mentally?
Comparing Fractions.answer: Writing out all converted forms together (all with the same denominator) lets you visually scan and compare ALL the numerators at once, reducing the mental effort and risk of error compared to trying to remember and compare values one pair at a time.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: What are the two steps to find a fraction of a quantity?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: Divide the quantity by the denominator, then multiply the result by the numerator.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: What is 1/4 of 28?
What is 1/5 of 35?
What is 2/3 of 18?
What is 3/7 of 49?
A basket has 24 fruits. If 1/6 are oranges, how many oranges are there?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: 24÷6=4. So there are 4 oranges.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: A school has 50 students. If 3/5 are girls, how many girls are there?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: 50÷5=10, then 10×3=30. So there are 30 girls.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: Explain step by step how to find 5/8 of 32.
Explain step by step how to find 4/9 of 63.
Why must we divide by the DENOMINATOR first, rather than the numerator, when finding a fraction of a quantity?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: The denominator tells us how many EQUAL parts to split the quantity into — dividing by it first creates the correct-sized groups, which we then count using the numerator.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: A 60-page book has 7/12 of its pages already read. How many pages have been read?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: 60÷12=5, then 5×7=35. So 35 pages have been read.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: A factory produces 144 items per day, and 5/8 pass quality control. How many items pass quality control?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: 144÷8=18, then 18×5=90. So 90 items pass quality control.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: Why does this method (divide then multiply) work for ANY proper or improper fraction of a quantity?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: Dividing by the denominator finds the value of ONE equal part, and multiplying by the numerator scales that up to however many parts are needed — this logic holds whether the numerator is smaller (proper) or larger (improper) than the denominator.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: A 75-minute class has 2/5 of the time spent on a lecture. How many minutes is that?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: 75÷5=15, then 15×2=30. So 30 minutes are spent on the lecture.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: A 96-student school has 3/4 attending a field trip. How many students are attending?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: 96÷4=24, then 24×3=72. So 72 students are attending.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: A 120-page notebook has 5/6 of its pages used. How many pages are used?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: 120÷6=20, then 20×5=100. So 100 pages are used.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: A 84km journey has 3/7 already travelled. How many km have been travelled?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: 84÷7=12, then 12×3=36. So 36km have been travelled.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: A 250-item warehouse stock has 2/5 sold this week. How many items were sold?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: 250÷5=50, then 50×2=100. So 100 items were sold.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: A shop offers 1/5 off a ₹450 item. What is the discount amount, and what is the final price?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: 450÷5=90 (discount). Final price: 450−90=360. So the discount is ₹90 and the final price is ₹360.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: A 64-litre tank has 7/8 filled with water. How many litres of water are in the tank?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: 64÷8=8, then 8×7=56. So 56 litres are in the tank.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: Explain step by step how to find 5/9 of 81.
A 180-student school has 2/9 in the school band. How many students are in the band?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: 180÷9=20, then 20×2=40. So 40 students are in the band.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: Why might a STORE use the "fraction of a quantity" method when calculating discounts on prices?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: Discounts are often expressed as fractions (or percentages, which are a type of fraction) of the original price — using this method lets the store quickly and accurately calculate exactly how much money to subtract from the original price.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: A 99-question test has 4/11 of the questions on algebra. How many questions are on algebra?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: 99÷11=9, then 9×4=36. So 36 questions are on algebra.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: A 56kg sack of rice has 3/8 used for a community kitchen. How many kg were used?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: 56÷8=7, then 7×3=21. So 21kg were used.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: Why would it be INCORRECT to simply multiply the quantity by the numerator first, without dividing by the denominator?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: Multiplying first (without dividing) would give a number far larger than the original quantity, since it skips the step of finding the correct EQUAL-PART size before scaling — this would not represent the actual fractional portion at all.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: A 132-item shipment has 7/12 already delivered. How many items have been delivered?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: 132÷12=11, then 11×7=77. So 77 items have been delivered.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: A 65-student class has 3/5 preferring outdoor sports. How many students prefer outdoor sports?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: 65÷5=13, then 13×3=39. So 39 students prefer outdoor sports.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: A 144-minute concert has 5/6 of the time spent on music, with the rest on speeches. How many minutes are spent on speeches?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: 144÷6=24, then 24×5=120 minutes on music. So 144−120=24 minutes are spent on speeches.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: A 210-acre farm has 4/7 used for wheat. How many acres are used for wheat, and how many acres are used for OTHER crops?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: 210÷7=30, then 30×4=120 acres for wheat. Other crops: 210−120=90 acres.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: A construction project has a ₹2,400,000 budget, with 5/8 allocated to materials. How much money (in rupees) is allocated to materials?
Why might large organizations (businesses, governments) use FRACTIONS (rather than just describing amounts directly) when planning and communicating budgets?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: Fractions allow flexible, proportional planning that scales naturally if the TOTAL budget changes — describing an allocation as "5/8 of the budget" remains meaningful and easy to recalculate even if the total budget amount changes, unlike a fixed rupee amount.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: A 168-hour week has 3/8 of the time spent sleeping (on average). How many hours per week are spent sleeping, and how many hours are spent AWAKE?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: 168÷8=21, then 21×3=63 hours sleeping. Awake: 168−63=105 hours.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: A charity raises ₹540,000, with 7/12 going directly to a relief fund and the rest to administrative costs. How much money (in rupees) goes to administrative costs?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: 540,000÷12=45,000, then 45,000×7=315,000 to the relief fund. Administrative costs: 540,000−315,000=225,000, so ₹225,000 goes to administrative costs.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: Why is it important for a charity to be ABLE to clearly calculate and communicate fractions like "7/12 to relief, 5/12 to admin" to its donors?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: Donors often want transparency about exactly how their contributions are used — clearly calculated fraction breakdowns help build trust by showing precisely how much of the total funding goes toward the charity’s core mission versus operational costs.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: A 360-degree pie chart represents a company’s expenses, with 5/12 of the chart (degrees) representing salaries. How many degrees of the pie chart represent salaries?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: 360÷12=30, then 30×5=150. So 150 degrees represent salaries.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: Why does the SAME "fraction of a quantity" method apply equally well to degrees in a pie chart, money in a budget, or pages in a book?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: The mathematical method does not depend on WHAT is being measured — it simply scales any total quantity according to a given fraction, so the underlying calculation works identically whether the "quantity" is degrees, money, pages, or anything else countable.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: A 480-student university department has 5/16 of students specializing in research. How many students specialize in research?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: 480÷16=30, then 30×5=150. So 150 students specialize in research.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: A 1,000-item inventory has 3/20 found to be defective during a quality check. How many items are defective, and how many are NOT defective?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: 1000÷20=50, then 50×3=150 defective items. Not defective: 1000−150=850 items.

Fraction of a Quantity.q: Why might companies want to track defect rates as a FRACTION (like 3/20) rather than just a raw count (like "150 items")?
Fraction of a Quantity.answer: A fraction (or the equivalent percentage) allows fair comparison across different batch sizes or time periods — "150 defective items" means something very different if the batch was 1,000 items versus 10,000 items, but the fraction 3/20 communicates the RATE consistently regardless of batch size.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: How do you add two like fractions?
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: Add the numerators and keep the denominator the same.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: How do you subtract two like fractions?
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: Subtract the numerators and keep the denominator the same.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: What is 3/8 + 2/8?
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: 3/8 + 2/8 = 5/8 (add numerators, keep denominator).

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: What is 5/9 + 2/9?

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: 7/10 − 3/10 = 4/10 (which simplifies to 2/5).

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: What is the first step when adding two unlike fractions?
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: Find the LCM of the denominators and convert both fractions to like fractions.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: Explain step by step how to solve 2/3 + 1/4.
steps: Find the LCM of 3 and 4: LCM=12.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: Explain step by step how to solve 5/6 − 1/4.
steps: Find the LCM of 6 and 4: LCM=12.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: Why must you convert unlike fractions to a COMMON denominator before adding or subtracting, instead of just adding/subtracting the numerators directly?
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: The denominator represents the SIZE of the parts being combined — if the parts are different sizes (different denominators), simply adding the numerators would combine unequal-sized pieces incorrectly, giving a wrong total.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: A jug has 3/4 litre of juice. If 1/4 litre is poured out, how much remains?
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: 3/4 − 1/4 = 2/4 (simplifies to 1/2) litre remains.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: Ravi ate 1/5 of a cake on Monday and 2/5 on Tuesday. What fraction of the cake did he eat in total?
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: 1/5 + 2/5 = 3/5 of the cake.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: A worker completed 3/8 of a job in the morning and 4/8 in the afternoon. What fraction of the job is complete?
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: 3/8 + 4/8 = 7/8 of the job is complete.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: A tank had 7/9 of its capacity filled. After using 2/9, how much remains?
Subtract 5/6 − 1/3 using LCM 6 (1/3=2/6).
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: 5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6 (simplifies to 1/2).
9/12 + 8/12 = 17/12 (an improper fraction, equal to 1 5/12).

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: Why can adding two unlike fractions sometimes give an IMPROPER fraction as the answer, even if both original fractions were proper?
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: If the sum of the converted numerators exceeds the common denominator, the result becomes greater than 1 whole, which is represented as an improper fraction (or equivalently, a mixed fraction).

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: Subtract 9/10 − 3/5 using LCM 10 (3/5=6/10).
A painter used 2/3 litre of blue paint and 1/6 litre of white paint. How much paint did the painter use in total? (Use LCM 6.)
A water tank started with 11/12 full and lost 1/4 due to a leak (using LCM 12: 1/4=3/12). How much water remains?
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: 11/12 − 3/12 = 8/12 (simplifies to 2/3) remains.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: When adding mixed fractions like 2 1/3 + 1 1/4, what is the recommended first step?
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: Convert both mixed fractions to improper fractions first: 2 1/3 = 7/3 and 1 1/4 = 5/4.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: Continuing the previous question, add 7/3 + 5/4 using LCM 12 (7/3=28/12, 5/4=15/12).
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: 28/12 + 15/12 = 43/12, which can be converted back to the mixed fraction 3 7/12.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: Subtract the mixed fractions 3 1/2 − 1 1/4 by first converting to improper fractions.
steps: Find LCM of 2 and 4: LCM=4. Convert 7/2 to fourths: 7/2=14/4.
Subtract: 14/4 − 5/4 = 9/4, which equals the mixed fraction 2 1/4.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: A recipe needs 1 1/2 cups of flour for the base and 2/3 cup for the topping. Find the total flour needed.
steps: Find LCM of 2 and 3: LCM=6. Convert: 3/2=9/6 and 2/3=4/6.
Add: 9/6 + 4/6 = 13/6, which equals the mixed fraction 2 1/6.
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: The recipe needs a total of 2 1/6 cups of flour.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: Why is it important to express the FINAL answer in its simplest form after adding or subtracting fractions?
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: A simplified answer is easier to understand, compare, and use in further calculations — leaving an unsimplified fraction (like 4/8 instead of 1/2) can make later steps more confusing than necessary.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: A shopkeeper sold 3/8 of his stock in the morning and 1/4 in the afternoon (using LCM 8: 1/4=2/8). What fraction of his stock did he sell in total?
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: 3/8 + 2/8 = 5/8 of his stock sold in total.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: Continuing the previous question, what fraction of the stock REMAINS unsold?
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: 1 − 5/8 = 8/8 − 5/8 = 3/8 of the stock remains unsold.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: A tailor cuts 5/6 metre from a 1-metre cloth piece for a shirt, then uses 1/12 metre more for a patch (using LCM 12: 5/6=10/12). What is the total cloth used?
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: 10/12 + 1/12 = 11/12 metre used in total.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: A 2 3/5 km path is divided so a runner completes 1 1/5 km first. Find the remaining distance using improper fractions.
steps: Since denominators are already the same, subtract directly: 13/5 − 6/5 = 7/5.
Convert back to a mixed fraction: 7/5 = 1 2/5.
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: The remaining distance is 1 2/5 km.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: A construction site needs 4 1/4 tonnes of sand for a foundation and 2 5/8 tonnes for a wall. Find the total sand needed.
steps: Find LCM of 4 and 8: LCM=8. Convert 17/4 to eighths: 17/4=34/8.
Add: 34/8 + 21/8 = 55/8, which equals the mixed fraction 6 7/8.
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: The total sand needed is 6 7/8 tonnes.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: Why might construction or engineering projects need to add fraction quantities (like materials in tonnes or metres) with such PRECISION, rather than rounding to whole numbers?
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: Even small fractional differences in material amounts can lead to shortages, excess waste, or structural inaccuracies — precise fraction-based calculations help ensure the right amount of material is ordered and used.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: A 7 1/3 litre tank has 2 5/6 litres removed for testing. Find the remaining amount.
steps: Find LCM of 3 and 6: LCM=6. Convert 22/3 to sixths: 22/3=44/6.
Subtract: 44/6 − 17/6 = 27/6, which simplifies to the mixed fraction 4 1/2.
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: The remaining amount is 4 1/2 litres.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: A 3-stage relay race covers 2/5 km, 3/10 km, and 1/2 km respectively. Find the TOTAL race distance (use LCM 10).
steps: Write the total: 12/10, which simplifies to the mixed fraction 1 1/5.
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: The total race distance is 1 1/5 km.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: Why does adding THREE OR MORE unlike fractions (like in the previous relay race question) still follow exactly the same core method as adding just two unlike fractions?
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: The method of finding a common denominator (LCM of ALL denominators present) and adding all the converted numerators together scales naturally to any number of fractions, since every fraction is still being resized to the same common "unit" before combining.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: A 5 1/6 kg bag of rice has 1 3/4 kg removed, then 7/12 kg is added back. Find the final amount (use LCM 12 throughout).
steps: Add back: 41/12 + 7/12 = 48/12, which simplifies to exactly 4.
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: The final amount is exactly 4 kg.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: Why might a multi-step fraction problem (like the previous rice bag question) be SAFER to solve by converting EVERYTHING to the same denominator from the very start, rather than converting separately at each step?
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: Converting everything to one common denominator from the start avoids the need to repeatedly re-find and re-convert denominators at each step, reducing the chances of arithmetic errors across multiple calculation stages.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: A 9 5/8 metre rope is cut into pieces: first 3 1/4 metres, then 2 3/8 metres. Find the remaining rope length.
steps: Convert to improper fractions with denominator 8: 9 5/8=77/8, 3 1/4=26/8, 2 3/8=19/8.
Subtract the second piece: 51/8 − 19/8 = 32/8, which equals exactly 4.
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: The remaining rope length is exactly 4 metres.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: A scientist mixes 1 2/3 ml of solution A with 2 1/6 ml of solution B, then removes 5/6 ml for testing. Find the final volume.
steps: Subtract the removed amount: 23/6 − 5/6 = 18/6, which equals exactly 3.
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: The final volume is exactly 3 ml.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: Why does getting a WHOLE NUMBER answer (like exactly 3 or exactly 4) sometimes happen even after several fraction operations, as seen in recent questions?
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: A whole number result occurs whenever the final numerator happens to be an exact multiple of the denominator after all operations — this is simply a property of how the specific numbers in the problem combine, not a special rule unique to whole-number answers.

Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.q: A farmer harvests 3 1/2 tonnes of wheat from Field A and 2 3/4 tonnes from Field B, then sells 4 1/8 tonnes. How much wheat remains?
steps: Subtract the amount sold: 50/8 − 33/8 = 17/8, which equals the mixed fraction 2 1/8.
Addition & Subtraction of Fractions.answer: The remaining wheat is 2 1/8 tonnes.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: What clue word in a problem usually signals addition of fractions?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: Words like "altogether" or "in total" usually signal addition.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: What clue word in a problem usually signals subtraction of fractions?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: Words like "left" or "remaining" usually signal subtraction.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: What clue phrase usually signals finding a fraction OF a quantity?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: A phrase like "2/3 of [some quantity]" signals finding a fraction of that quantity (divide then multiply).

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: Ravi ate 2/7 of a pizza and his friend ate 3/7. What fraction did they eat altogether?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 2/7 + 3/7 = 5/7 of the pizza eaten altogether.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: A 9/10 full water bottle has 4/10 used. What fraction of water remains?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 9/10 − 4/10 = 5/10 (simplifies to 1/2) remains.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: A class of 45 students has 3/5 attending a workshop. How many students are attending?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 45÷5=9, then 9×3=27 students attending.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: A 20m ribbon has 1/4 cut off for one gift and 3/10 cut off for another (using LCM 20: 1/4=5/20, 3/10=6/20). What fraction of the ribbon has been cut off in total?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 5/20 + 6/20 = 11/20 of the ribbon cut off in total.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: Continuing the previous question, what fraction of the 20m ribbon REMAINS?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 20/20 − 11/20 = 9/20 of the ribbon remains.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: Explain step by step how to solve: a 50-litre tank loses 1/5 of its water, then 1/4 of what remains is used. How much water is used in the SECOND step?
steps: Find the first loss: 1/5 of 50 = 50÷5=10 litres lost.
Find 1/4 of the remaining: 40÷4=10 litres used in the second step.
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 10 litres are used in the second step.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: A 36-question quiz has 1/4 answered wrong. How many questions were answered correctly?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 36÷4=9 answered wrong. Correct: 36−9=27 questions.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: Why is it useful to identify EXACTLY what a word problem is asking for BEFORE starting any calculations?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: Word problems often contain extra numbers or steps — clearly identifying the final question first helps you choose the right operations and avoid wasting time calculating something that is not actually needed for the answer.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: A 64-page comic book has 3/8 read on day one and 1/4 read on day two (using LCM 8: 1/4=2/8). What fraction has been read after TWO days?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 3/8 + 2/8 = 5/8 of the comic book read after two days.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: Continuing the previous question, how many of the 64 pages have been read (5/8 of 64)?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 64÷8=8, then 8×5=40 pages read.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: A 72-student class has 5/9 playing cricket and 2/9 playing football, with the rest doing other activities. What fraction does OTHER activities represent?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 5/9+2/9=7/9 play cricket or football, leaving 9/9−7/9=2/9 for other activities.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: Continuing the previous question, how many of the 72 students do OTHER activities (2/9 of 72)?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 72÷9=8, then 8×2=16 students.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: A 48m wall is painted: 1/3 on day one, then 1/4 of the REMAINING wall on day two. How many metres are painted on day one?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 1/3 of 48 = 48÷3=16 metres painted on day one.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: Continuing the previous question, how many metres of wall remain after day one (48m wall, 16m painted)?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 48−16=32 metres remain after day one.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: Continuing the previous question, how many metres are painted on day TWO (1/4 of the remaining 32m)?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 32÷4=8 metres painted on day two.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: Continuing the previous question, how many total metres of the 48m wall are painted after BOTH days (16m + 8m)?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 16+8=24 metres painted in total after both days.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: A 90-minute movie has 2/5 watched on a flight and 3/10 watched at home (using LCM 10: 2/5=4/10). What fraction of the movie has been watched in total?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 4/10 + 3/10 = 7/10 of the movie watched in total.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: Continuing the previous question, how many minutes of the 90-minute movie have been watched (7/10 of 90)?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 90÷10=9, then 9×7=63 minutes watched.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: A shopkeeper has 80kg of rice. He sells 3/8 in the morning and 1/4 in the afternoon (using LCM 8: 1/4=2/8). What fraction of rice REMAINS unsold?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 3/8+2/8=5/8 sold, leaving 8/8−5/8=3/8 unsold.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: Continuing the previous question, how many kg of rice remain unsold (3/8 of 80kg)?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 80÷8=10, then 10×3=30kg remain unsold.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: Why might solving a long word problem in clearly LABELED steps (Step 1, Step 2, etc.) help avoid mistakes, compared to trying to do all the math in your head at once?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: Labeling each step keeps track of WHAT each calculated number represents (like "rope cut" versus "rope remaining"), reducing the risk of accidentally using the wrong number in a later step or losing track of the overall problem.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: A 56-page report has 1/8 written on Monday, 1/4 written on Tuesday (using LCM 8: 1/4=2/8), and the rest on Wednesday. What fraction is written on Wednesday?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 1/8+2/8=3/8 written by Tuesday, leaving 8/8−3/8=5/8 for Wednesday.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: Continuing the previous question, how many of the 56 pages are written on Wednesday (5/8 of 56)?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 56÷8=7, then 7×5=35 pages written on Wednesday.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: A school organizes a fun day with a ₹150,000 budget. 2/5 is spent on games, 3/10 on food (using LCM 10: 2/5=4/10), and the rest on decorations. Find the fraction spent on decorations, showing your steps.
steps: Subtract from the whole: 10/10−7/10=3/10 for decorations.
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 3/10 of the budget is spent on decorations.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: Continuing the previous question, how much money (in rupees) is spent on decorations if it is 3/10 of ₹150,000?
A 96km road trip is split into three legs: 1/4 of the distance, then 1/3 of the REMAINING distance, with the rest being the final leg. Find the distance of the FIRST leg.
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 1/4 of 96 = 96÷4=24km for the first leg.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: Continuing the previous question, how many km remain after the FIRST leg (96km total, 24km done)?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 96−24=72km remain after the first leg.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: Continuing the previous question, how many km is the SECOND leg (1/3 of the remaining 72km)?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 72÷3=24km for the second leg.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: Continuing the previous question, how many km is the FINAL (third) leg of the 96km trip?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: After 24km (leg 1) and 24km (leg 2), total so far is 24+24=48km. Final leg: 96−48=48km.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: A factory produces 720 units. 5/12 are sold domestically, 1/4 are exported (using LCM 12: 1/4=3/12), and the rest remain in storage. Find the fraction remaining in storage.
steps: Subtract from the whole: 12/12−8/12=4/12 remaining in storage.
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 4/12 (which simplifies to 1/3) of the units remain in storage.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: Continuing the previous question, how many of the 720 units remain in storage (1/3 of 720)?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 720÷3=240 units remain in storage.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: A charity event collects ₹360,000 in donations. 1/6 comes from a single large donor, 5/12 from a fundraiser (using LCM 12: 1/6=2/12), and the rest from small individual donations. What fraction comes from small individual donations?
steps: Subtract from the whole: 12/12−7/12=5/12 from small donations.
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 5/12 of the donations come from small individual donations.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: Continuing the previous question, how much money (in rupees) comes from small individual donations if it is 5/12 of ₹360,000?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: 360,000÷12=30,000, then 30,000×5=150,000. So ₹150,000 comes from small individual donations.

Word Problems / Mixed Practice.q: Why does solving a complex, multi-part word problem (like the charity donation example) require combining SEVERAL fraction skills together — addition, subtraction, AND finding a fraction of a quantity?
Word Problems / Mixed Practice.answer: Real-world situations rarely involve just ONE isolated fraction operation — they typically require first combining given fractions (addition), finding what is left (subtraction), and then converting the resulting fraction into an actual real-world quantity (fraction of a quantity), which is why mastering all these skills together is so valuable.

Tenths & Hundredths.q: What does the decimal point do in a number like 7.2?
Tenths & Hundredths.answer: It separates the whole number part (7) from the decimal part (2).

Tenths & Hundredths.q: Write 3/10 as a decimal.
Write 9/100 as a decimal.
In the decimal 4.56, name the place value of each digit after the dot.

Tenths & Hundredths.q: A strip of 10 equal boxes has 8 shaded. Write this as a fraction and as a decimal.
A 10x10 grid of 100 squares has 34 shaded. Write this as a decimal.
Why does 0.05 need a zero right after the decimal point?
Tenths & Hundredths.answer: Because there are no full tenths (only 5 hundredths), so a zero must hold the tenths place to keep the value correct.

Tenths & Hundredths.q: Read the decimal 6.08 in words.
